Extend cycle detection to emit a topological order — push nodes as they finish in DFS post-order then reverse, or dequeue them in Kahn's order — while still catching cycles. Hit the O(V + E) target.
levels.teaches: Topological sort as the PAYLOAD of the same traversal rather than a new algorithm; DFS post-order-reversed versus Kahn's dequeue order; that a valid ordering exists if and only if there is no cycle, all discovered in one linear pass.

levels.name: The Ladder
levels.problem: Word Ladder: transform beginWord into endWord one letter at a time, with every intermediate word in the dictionary, returning the shortest transformation length. Fuse this chapter's BFS-shortest-path engine with the arrays-hashing pattern: pre-index the word list into a hash map of wildcard patterns (e.g. 'h*t' -> [hot, hit]) for O(1) neighbor generation plus a hash set of seen words, then BFS from beginWord counting levels until you reach endWord.
levels.teaches: Modeling a non-obvious problem AS a graph (words are nodes, single-letter edits are edges); combining BFS-for-shortest-path with hash-based adjacency generation and O(1) membership from arrays-hashing; the full pipeline — build adjacency, seed the queue, ripple out level by level, and stop the instant you reach the target.

fullChapters.title: Dynamic Programming — The Memo Tape
fullChapters.oneLineGoal: Turn slow, self-repeating recursion into fast table-filling by spotting overlapping subproblems and caching each subproblem's answer exactly once.
fullChapters.mechanismInOneSentence: Many problems recompute the same subproblem exponentially often; DP stores each subproblem's answer once on a memo tape and builds bigger answers from already-solved smaller ones, turning brown-out exponential recursion into fast linear table-filling.

levels.name: The Recompute Trap
levels.problem: Fibonacci (mechanism primer): poke a naive recursive fib(n) and watch the call-tree robots re-scan the same numbered crates over and over as the brown-out power meter spikes red; then flip the MEMO TAPE lever and watch every repeat call get answered instantly from a cache crate, the tree collapsing and the meter going green.
levels.teaches: Overlapping subproblems: naive recursion redoes identical work exponentially, while a memo (cache) makes each subproblem cost once — the entire reason DP exists.

levels.name: Climb the Tape
levels.problem: Climbing Stairs (LC 70): watch a bottom-up solution fill a tape of crates left to right, each crate dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], with two robots reading the two crates just behind them.
levels.teaches: Writing a recurrence and filling a 1-D DP table bottom-up (tabulation), reading only from already-solved smaller crates instead of recursing.

levels.name: Cheapest Steps
levels.problem: Min Cost Climbing Stairs (LC 746): watch the tape fill where each crate takes the cheaper of its two predecessors plus that step's cost, dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]).
levels.teaches: A DP transition that chooses the best (min) among options and accumulates a cost — DP as picking the best predecessor, not just summing neighbors.

levels.name: Rob the Street
levels.problem: House Robber (LC 198): the tape and robots are wired up except one crate's formula is blank — fill the transition dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2]) so the robber takes the best of skip-this-house versus rob-this-house-plus-two-back.
levels.teaches: The take-or-skip decision: each cell is a max over 'use this element' vs 'don't', with the no-adjacent constraint encoded by reaching back to i-2.

levels.name: The Ring of Houses
levels.problem: House Robber II (LC 213): houses sit on a circle so the first and last are now adjacent; fill the wiring that runs your House-Robber solver twice — once on houses[0..n-2], once on houses[1..n-1] — and returns the max of the two.
levels.teaches: Reducing a new constraint (a circular street) to a problem you already solved by splitting it into two linear subproblems.

levels.name: Break the Word
levels.problem: Word Break (LC 139): write it cold. Over a tape indexed by string position, dp[i] is reachable if some earlier reachable crate j has s[j:i] in the word set; return dp[len(s)].
levels.teaches: Boolean reachability DP over a string, using an inner scan back to earlier crates plus O(1) hash-set membership for the dictionary lookup.

levels.name: Make the Change
levels.problem: Coin Change (LC 322): write it cold. Build a tape indexed by AMOUNT rather than by position; dp[a] = min over coins c of dp[a-c] + 1, holding unreachable amounts at an infinity sentinel and returning dp[amount] or -1.
levels.teaches: DP over a value/amount axis with unbounded reuse of choices, minimizing a count, and using an infinity sentinel to mark impossible cells.

levels.name: Decode Under Pressure
levels.problem: Decode Ways (LC 91): you're handed a correct but exponential recursion that branches on take-one-digit versus take-two-digits and browns out on a long digit string; add a memo (or convert to an O(n) tape) to clear the power meter — while handling '0', valid '10'/'20', and invalid '30'.
levels.teaches: Recognizing overlapping subproblems in a fresh problem and applying the memo mechanism yourself to collapse exponential recursion to O(n) — the primer's lesson, now self-driven, with careful transition edge cases.

levels.name: The Longest Climb
levels.problem: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LC 300): write the O(n^2) DP cold — dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for all j<i with nums[j] < nums[i]), and the answer is max(dp).
levels.teaches: Subsequence DP where each crate depends on ALL earlier crates (not just fixed neighbors), scanning back to extend the best compatible increasing run.

levels.name: Patience Under Brown-Out
levels.problem: Longest Increasing Subsequence, O(n log n) (LC 300): the O(n^2) inner scan browns out on a huge array; maintain a 'tails' tape and, for each number, BINARY-SEARCH the first tail >= it and overwrite it (patience sorting), hitting O(n log n) to beat the tighter power meter.
levels.teaches: Fusing DP thinking with binary search: replace the O(n) inner scan with a binary-searched tails array to solve the same problem from the open level, now optimally.

fullChapters.title: Intervals: Sort, Sweep, and the Frontier
fullChapters.oneLineGoal: Kill the O(n^2) "compare every pair" instinct: sort intervals by a boundary, then sweep once to detect overlaps, merge bars, and count rooms.
fullChapters.mechanismInOneSentence: Sort intervals by one boundary, then sweep left-to-right exactly once, deciding every overlap and merge by comparing the current interval's edge to a running frontier (the furthest end seen so far).

levels.name: The Overlap Lamp
levels.problem: Sandbox: two draggable interval bars sharing one number line. Drag their endpoints through presets (disjoint, touching at an endpoint, partial overlap, one nested inside the other); an 'overlap lamp' lights and highlights the shared region whenever they intersect. No code, no fail.
levels.teaches: An interval is a [start, end] bar on a timeline; two bars overlap exactly when a.start <= b.end AND b.start <= a.end; the tricky endpoint-touch case ([1,2] vs [2,3]) and why < vs <= is the whole decision.

levels.name: Sort, Then Sweep
levels.problem: Meeting Rooms I — given meeting [start, end] intervals, return True if one person can attend them all (no two overlap). Watch the tracer: crates reorder as it sorts by start, then a robot sweeps left-to-right comparing each start against the previous meeting's end; the first collision flips the lamp to False.
levels.teaches: Sorting by start collapses 'compare everyone to everyone' (O(n^2)) into a single O(n log n) sweep; once sorted, an overlap can only happen with the immediately previous interval, so you only ever compare curr.start to prev.end.

levels.name: Does It Fit?
levels.problem: Meeting Rooms I again, with the overlap test blanked out. Fill the single line inside the loop: the condition on intervals[i][0] and intervals[i-1][1] that returns False when two sorted meetings collide.
levels.teaches: Writing the overlap comparison against the running previous end; choosing < vs <= so that back-to-back meetings ([1,2],[2,3]) are allowed while genuine overlaps are caught.

levels.name: The Frontier Robot
levels.problem: Merge Intervals — merge all overlapping intervals into the fewest bars. Watch: after sorting by start, a 'current merged bar' grows rightward; when the next bar overlaps, the frontier end becomes max(frontier end, next end); when a gap appears, the finished bar is emitted to the output tape and a fresh one begins.
levels.teaches: Carrying a running merged interval (the frontier) instead of comparing pairs; extend-with-max on the end (a later bar can be shorter, so you MUST take max, not just overwrite); emit-on-gap to close out a merged run.

levels.name: Collapse the Bars
levels.problem: Merge Intervals — write it cold: sort by start, keep a result list, and for each interval either extend the last result bar (when it overlaps) or append a new one. Return the merged list.
levels.teaches: Owning the full sort + sweep + merge loop end to end; the append-vs-extend branch; using result[-1] as the live frontier so you never need a separate tracking variable.

levels.name: Slot It In
levels.problem: Insert Interval — given an already sorted, non-overlapping list plus one newInterval, return the list with newInterval inserted and merged. Write it as three passes: copy every interval that ends before newInterval starts, absorb every interval that overlaps newInterval (widening it), then copy the rest.
levels.teaches: Exploiting input that is ALREADY sorted so no sort is needed (O(n), not O(n log n)); the three-region sweep (strictly-left / overlapping / strictly-right); merging a single moving bar by taking min of starts and max of ends.

levels.name: Fewest to Cut
levels.problem: Non-overlapping Intervals — return the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest don't overlap. A sort-by-start, keep-the-newest attempt browns out on adversarial inputs; hit the target by sorting on END and greedily keeping the interval that finishes earliest, dropping any whose start lands before that finish.
levels.teaches: Greedy interval scheduling: sort by END (not start) so the earliest-finishing bar leaves the most room for later ones; each kept interval's end becomes the new frontier; a drop = a removal. Cements the judgment call of when to sort by start vs by end (builds on the Greedy chapter).

levels.name: How Many Rooms?
levels.problem: Meeting Rooms II — return the minimum number of rooms so no two meetings share one. Sort by start, sweep the meetings, and keep a min-heap of the end times of meetings still in progress: before each new meeting, pop every room whose end <= this start (freed up), then push this meeting's end; the peak heap size is the answer.
levels.teaches: Fusing the interval sweep with a heap: the min-heap holds the frontier of all currently-open meetings, and its smallest end is the soonest a room frees; peak heap size = max concurrent overlaps = rooms needed. Combines the Intervals sweep with the Heaps pattern.

fullChapters.title: Greedy: Commit and Never Look Back
fullChapters.oneLineGoal: Recognize when a single forward sweep that commits to the locally best move — and never backtracks — beats searching every option.
fullChapters.mechanismInOneSentence: At each step commit to the choice that looks best right now and never undo it, carrying one running "best"/"frontier" register through a single forward pass, trusting that locally optimal moves compound into the global optimum.

levels.name: The Committed Robot
levels.problem: Poke-and-watch (no fail): a hauler robot walks a tape of crates holding mixed +/- values, carrying a 'haul' battery. At each crate you poke to watch it make one choice — extend the current haul (add this crate) or dump it and restart from here — while a separate 'best haul ever' ledger quietly records the maximum. Watch the running total get dumped the instant carrying it would hurt. This is Maximum Subarray seen from zero, with no code to write.
levels.teaches: The greedy contract itself: one forward pass, an irreversible local choice at each crate, and a single running-best register — you never walk backward or reconsider a crate.

levels.name: Best Haul on the Tape
levels.problem: Maximum Subarray (NeetCode). Watch the tracer run Kadane's algorithm on the crate tape: cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur). Use the scrubber to see cur reset to the current crate's value the moment carrying the old prefix sum would drag it down.
levels.teaches: Kadane's greedy rule — drop the running sum the instant it goes negative, since a negative prefix can only shrink any future haul; keep the global best in a separate register.

levels.name: The Reach Frontier
levels.problem: Jump Game (NeetCode). A robot must decide if it can reach the last crate, where each crate's number is its maximum jump length. Fill the one missing line that extends the reachable frontier: reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]); the surrounding code already bails if index i ever passes reach.
levels.teaches: Feasibility greedy — keep only the single farthest index you can reach; as long as the current index sits inside reach, the frontier can always be pushed further, so no branching search is needed.

levels.name: Trim the Overshoot
levels.problem: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet (NeetCode). Fill the guard line that discards any triplet exceeding the target in any position — if a <= t[0] and b <= t[1] and c <= t[2] — so that only harmless triplets get OR-max'd position-by-position into the target.
levels.teaches: A second greedy flavor, filter-then-accumulate: throw away every candidate that could never help (it overshoots somewhere), then safely combine what remains without any backtracking.

levels.name: Clean Cuts
levels.problem: Partition Labels (NeetCode). Write it cold: precompute each character's last index into a hash map, then sweep the string expanding the current segment's end via end = max(end, last[c]); cut a partition the moment the index reaches that end, then start the next segment fresh.
levels.teaches: Greedy boundary-growing — grow a window only as far as the farthest obligation inside it forces you to, then commit the cut and never merge backward; the last-occurrence map turns a search into one sweep.

levels.name: Fewest Leaps
levels.problem: Jump Game II (NeetCode). Write the minimum-jumps solver cold: track the end of the current jump's range and the farthest index reachable within it; when the index hits the range end, spend one jump and push the range out to farthest. Return the jump count.
levels.teaches: Optimization greedy as level-by-level (BFS-by-range) expansion — you never choose which crate to land on; you only count a jump when the current reach is exhausted, always extending to the best frontier seen so far.

levels.name: One Loop, No Retries
levels.problem: Gas Station (NeetCode). The obvious 'try starting at every station' is O(n^2) and browns out the power meter on large tapes. Hit the O(n) target: if total gas >= total cost a solution exists, and the answer is the station right after wherever the running tank last dipped below zero.
levels.teaches: Collapsing an O(n^2) search into one greedy pass — any prefix whose tank goes negative can never be a valid start, so reset the candidate start there instead of re-scanning, justified by a single global feasibility check.

levels.name: Deal the Straights
levels.problem: Hand of Straights (NeetCode). Count every card into a hash map, then repeatedly pull the smallest available value off a min-heap and greedily build a run of groupSize consecutive cards, decrementing counts as you go; fail if any needed consecutive card is missing or its supply runs out. Fuses greedy commitment with a heap-driven 'always take the minimum' substrate feeding a Counter of supply.
levels.teaches: Boss fusion of greedy + heaps — the smallest remaining card is forced to start a group, so a min-heap keeps handing you the one correct irreversible move while a Counter tracks remaining supply; combine the running-frontier discipline from earlier levels with a priority-queue as the decision engine.

## 2. Cross-chapter difficulty curve

**Shape: a rising sawtooth, not a straight line.** Every chapter opens with a difficulty-1 (occasionally d2) *no-fail poke-and-watch primer* that rebuilds its mechanism from zero, then ramps 1→5 to a boss. So the *mechanical* floor resets to zero at each chapter boundary while the *conceptual* ceiling climbs. This reset is the single most important anti-cliff device in the design — an "advanced" chapter never demands you be advanced to *enter* it. This holds for all 15 chapters (verified: every `order:1` level is a primer at d1, plus deliberate mid-chapter primer/tutorial resets at Stack L6, Trees L8, Graphs L9).

**Within-chapter ramps are all monotone or dip-then-rise (dips are intentional).** No chapter jumps more than +1 difficulty between consecutive levels except across a deliberate new-mechanic reset (Stack's monotonic-wall primer, Trees' BFS tutorial, Graphs' Rotting-Oranges tutorial), which *lower* difficulty to introduce a fresh tool — the correct direction.

**The conceptual ceiling is raised gradually by pre-planted bridges, not by the primers.** The design already threads each hard idea one chapter early so its "home" chapter is a re-grounding, not a first contact:
- **Memoization** is introduced in Recursion L9 (Cache the Tree) and is the entire premise of DP L1 — DP does not spring memoization on a beginner.
- **Two-pointer merge** appears in Recursion L10 (Merge Sort) and is reused by Binary Search L10 and DP thinking.
- **Grid DFS + un-mark** is taught in Backtracking L10 (Word Search) before Tries' Word Search II boss.
- **BFS/queue** is seeded in Trees L8 before it becomes the spine of Graphs.
- **Sort-by-a-boundary greedy** is taught in Greedy before Intervals L7 explicitly leans on it.

This is what keeps the ceiling smooth. I want it preserved and made explicit in build tickets.

**Genuine risk points and fixes:**

1. **The recursion pivot (Act I → Recursion) is the steepest *conceptual* transition** — all of Act I is iterative loops; Recursion demands a new mental model. Mechanically it's soft (primer d1), and it's well-bridged (call-stack primer explicitly reuses the Stack substrate; Recursion L5 recurses over the linked list the learner just built). **Verdict: adequately bridged — do not add a level, but protect L1 (Tower of Frames) and L5 (Recurse Down the Chain) polish; they carry the transition.** Also keep Linked List immediately before Recursion (they're adjacent at #6→#7) so L6/L7 recursion problems reuse fresh material.

2. **DP open levels are the highest cliff risk.** The ramp is generous through L5 (House Robber II, guided), then L6 Word Break is the first *open* DP whose recurrence isn't "look one or two cells back" — it needs an inner scan back over all earlier cells plus set membership. That's a real jump from the fixed-neighbor transitions before it. **Fix: insert a bridge level DP-L6a "Word Break, Watched" (tutorial) before the cold Word Break** — a watch-and-scrub run of the dp[i] reachability sweep so the inner-loop-over-earlier-cells shape is seen before it's written. Cheap, high payoff.

3. **Graphs L11→L12: directed graphs + cycle detection is a new concept dropped straight into an *open* level.** Everything before L12 is undirected reachability; Course Schedule introduces edge direction, the 3-color on-path marker, and Kahn's indegree engine at once. **Fix: insert a bridge level Graphs-L11a "Watch the Cycle" (tutorial)** — a scrub-through of DFS 3-color marking on a tiny directed graph, showing a back-edge lighting red, before Course Schedule is written cold.

4. **Legit hard d5 bosses (accept as-is):** Median of Two Sorted Arrays (Binary Search), Word Ladder / Course Schedule II (Graphs), LRU Cache (Linked List). These are supposed to be steep — they're bosses gated behind a full internal ramp and a fusion the learner has already rehearsed. No fix; just make sure the "beat the brown-out" target is the last gate, not correctness alone.

5. **Graphs is the longest chapter (14, now 15 levels) with two d5 bosses.** Not a cliff — a pacing note. Consider surfacing it as two visible sub-arcs in the UI (Grid Flood-Fill L1–L11, Directed/Dependency L12–L14) so it doesn't read as a slog.

A single `curriculum.json` the Flutter app reads at boot. Three nested record types. IDs are stable slugs; the app resolves prereqs and lock state client-side.
